attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, in his authorial voice.

semantics.note: 'Always going to require' for at least a decade or two is a firm forecast. 'Probably more' is a hedged extension and is correctly left with no deadline. The proposition keeps the minimum duration and the scope 'big projects'.

contract.note: Reading architects as a function and big projects as substantial systems is ordinary and fair. Requiring necessity rather than mere employment is fair. The 'decade or two' window is ambiguous, but the contract handles it with an early-contradiction rule set at 2035.

evidence.note: Epoch's MirrorCode reimplements CLI programs autonomously against precise specifications and test cases. Epoch itself notes this is unlike real development. It is not a substantial real project built without human architectural input.

A first-person account of AI-built back-office tooling with no traditional developers. The owner still made the architecture and control choices, and the success is not independently verified. Not a qualifying counterexample.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast running to at least 2035, and that deadline has not passed. The early-resolution rule needs a verified substantial project completed without competent human architectural input. Neither item meets that bar: e1 is a narrow benchmark, and e2 involved human design choices and is unverified. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'often', the approximate 80/20 framing and the driverless-car example. It is a historical generalisation, so observation is correct.

contract.note: Reading 80/20 as a development heuristic rather than a literal ratio is a fair, ordinary reading. Because 'easy' and 'extremely difficult' have no defined measures, the result depends on how the effort comparison is interpreted.

evidence.note: CMU's account shows a computer drove more than 98% of a 1995 trip. That is substantial early functionality decades before the post, though only for steering, with humans controlling speed and braking. It does not measure engineering effort.
A 2024 peer-reviewed comment explains why rare safety-critical cases remain hard for self-driving systems. This supports the residual-difficulty part for driving only.
A Waymo disclosure reports large-scale driverless rides in limited areas by 2024. This shows real progress but does not settle relative effort or the remaining long tail.

reviews.rationale: For driving, the evidence fits: substantial autonomy in 1995 (e1) and still-hard rare cases in 2024 (e2). But the support condition also needs representative evidence across AI, and a comparison of effort, beyond one industry. The packet has neither. The broader claim is left unsettled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement about Roose's app.

semantics.note: The firm part says the idea was not original and code for it already existed. The proposition keeps 'presumably' on the training inference, which is a hedge and not a scorable commitment.

contract.note: The contract requires training-provenance evidence for support and leaves the claim unresolved without it. That scores the explicitly hedged 'presumably trained' inference. Under policy the hedged part is not scored, so only the firm existence claim should decide the outcome.

evidence.note: A 2020 Deep-food repository revision describes recognising ingredients from a fridge photo and recommending recipes. It shows predecessor code existed well before March 2025. First public visibility rests on commit dates.

reviews.rationale: The firm claim, that the recipe-from-photo idea already existed in code, is supported by the dated Deep-food repository (e1). The training statement is hedged ('presumably'), so it is not adjudicable and is not scored. The contract's demand for training records wrongly scores that hedge.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement summarising a reported evaluation result.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'on one standardized measure', the GPT-4.5 target and the over-one-third threshold.

contract.note: Identifying the measure as the SimpleQA hallucination rate from the launch evaluation is the obvious reading. The strict over-33.3% threshold is fair.

evidence.note: Computerworld reports GPT-4.5's SimpleQA hallucination rate as 37.1%, which is over one third. This is secondary reporting of OpenAI's own result. That is enough to establish what was reported.
OpenAI's launch page confirms a SimpleQA hallucination-rate chart for GPT-4.5. The numbers could not be read from the extracted text.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's launch evaluation charted a SimpleQA hallucination rate for GPT-4.5 (e2), and reputable reporting gives that rate as 37.1% (e1). That is above one third on one standardized measure, as Marcus stated. The source is a company disclosure relayed by secondary reporting, which is adequate for a claim about what was reported.
